result: The authors conducted a cross-fostering experiment using 42 BXD recombinant inbred mouse lines and C57BL/6J (B6) mice to investigate genetic effects on parent-offspring interactions. The experimental design involved cross-fostering entire litters within 24h of birth, with genetically variable BXD mothers fostering genetically uniform B6 offspring and vice versa, allowing independent analysis of maternal and offspring genetic effects while controlling for the other. Behavioral observations and weight measurements were collected on postnatal days 6, 10, and 14 following established protocols.
evaluation: The experimental design is well-described with appropriate methodological details (C9-C18, C78-C97). The cross-fostering approach is validated by prior work (C15-C16) and the sample size justification is provided with power calculations (C72-C74). The BXD population characteristics are appropriately documented (C67-C69) and behavioral protocols follow established methods with proper citations.

result: Offspring genotype indirectly affects maternal nestbuilding behavior during the first postnatal week. A locus on offspring chromosome 7 (OspIge7.1) was mapped that modifies maternal nestbuilding on day 6, with the D2 allele increasing nestbuilding activity in B6 mothers fostering BXD pups. This behavior is particularly important for offspring fitness as thermoregulation is underdeveloped in early postnatal life.
evaluation: The genetic mapping result (C21-C22) is supported by Figure 2 showing genome-wide significant QTL. The biological importance of nestbuilding (C23) is appropriately cited. The indirect genetic effect is clearly demonstrated through the cross-fostering design where genetically uniform B6 mothers show differential behavior based on offspring genotype (C19-C20).

result: A locus on offspring distal chromosome 5 (OspIge5.1) affects maternal behavior on day 14, around the time of peak weaning conflict. Mothers showed increased levels of maternal behavior when fostering BXD offspring carrying the D2 allele at this locus.
evaluation: The genetic mapping result (C24, C26) is supported by Figure 3 showing a genome-wide significant QTL. The timing interpretation (C25) is consistent with developmental biology of mouse weaning. This represents a second independent indirect genetic effect locus affecting maternal behavior.

result: Maternal genotype indirectly affects offspring growth during the second postnatal week. A locus on maternal chromosome 17 (MatIge17.1) was identified where the B6 allele increases offspring growth, demonstrating that maternal genetic variation influences offspring phenotype independent of offspring genotype.
evaluation: The genetic mapping result (C27-C28) is supported by Figure 4 showing a genome-wide significant QTL. This demonstrates the reciprocal indirect genetic effect where maternal genotype affects offspring traits while offspring genotype is held constant through the cross-fostering design.

result: Direct genetic effect loci were identified for maternal behaviors and offspring solicitation. Maternal behavior mapped to chromosome 10 (MatDge10.1) and nestbuilding to chromosome 1 (MatDge1.1), with B6 alleles increasing trait values. Offspring solicitation behavior mapped to chromosome 5 (OspDge5.1) with the D2 allele increasing solicitation, located at the opposite end from the indirect effect locus OspIge5.1.
evaluation: While these direct genetic effects are reported (C29-C33), the manuscript does not provide figures or detailed statistical support for these QTL. Table 1 shows that MatDge1.1 has a suggestive (p=0.069) rather than genome-wide significant p-value, and MatDge10.1 is significant (p=0.008). The distinction between direct and indirect effects at different locations on chromosome 5 (C33) is noted but not fully explored.

result: The study demonstrates that both indirect genetic effects (IGEs) and direct genetic effects (DGEs) can be linked to specific loci affecting parent-offspring interactions. Genes expressed in offspring can indirectly influence maternal behavior and offspring fitness, while maternal genotype can indirectly modify offspring traits, showing that IGEs are an important component of the genetic architecture of complex traits.
evaluation: This conclusion (C34-C35, C57-C59) is well-supported by the multiple QTL mapping results showing both offspring-to-mother effects (C21-C26) and mother-to-offspring effects (C27-C28). The interpretation that selection may occur on these loci (C35) is appropriately cautious. The citation to Bijma and Wade (2008) provides theoretical context (C59).

result: Phenotypic correlations support the genetic mapping results showing offspring genotype affects maternal behavior. Offspring solicitation behavior in genetically variable BXD pups is positively correlated with maternal behavior in their genetically uniform B6 adoptive mothers on all three measurement days (day 6: r=0.56, p=0.003; day 10: r=0.63, p=0.001; day 14: r=0.55, p=0.008), with significant effects of maternal behavior and day on offspring solicitation (GLM, F1,103=17.62, p<0.001 and F2,103=14.22, p<0.001).
evaluation: The statistical analyses (C37-C41) provide strong phenotypic support for the genetic mapping results. The correlations are moderate to strong and highly significant across all three time points. The GLM analysis (C38) appropriately tests for effects of maternal behavior and developmental time. This phenotypic validation strengthens the genetic findings.

result: Maternal behavior influences offspring solicitation in genetically uniform offspring. When offspring genotype is held constant (B6), maternal behavior and day have significant positive effects on offspring solicitation (GLM, F1,118=6.33, p=0.013, and F2,118=6.33, p<0.001), demonstrating that variation in maternal genotype drives differences in offspring behavior.
evaluation: The statistical analysis (C42) supports the interpretation (C43) that maternal behavior influences offspring solicitation. The experimental design logic is sound: with no genetic variation in offspring, behavioral differences must arise from maternal genotype differences. This demonstrates the reciprocal nature of parent-offspring interactions.

result: A negative correlation exists between maternal provisioning and offspring solicitation in biological families. BXD offspring short-term weight gain negatively correlates with their biological mother's provisioning on day 10 (GLM, F1,32=4.77, p=0.036; r=-0.34), and offspring solicitation negatively correlates with maternal provisioning on day 14 (GLM, F1,28=8.046, p=0.008, r=-0.48). This suggests mothers who are generous providers produce offspring that solicit less, consistent with theoretical predictions when maternal traits are under selection.
evaluation: The statistical analyses (C48-C49) show significant negative correlations supported by Figure 5. The interpretation (C50) is reasonable and the theoretical context (C51) is appropriately cited to Kölliker et al. (2005). The negative correlation contrasts with some prior studies but is consistent with others (C45-C46), and the authors provide appropriate theoretical justification.

result: Offspring solicitation behavior is costly, as evidenced by a negative correlation between bodyweight and solicitation level. The overall effect is highly significant (GLM, F1,66=20.57, p<0.001), with negative correlations on day 10 (r=-0.39) and day 14 (r=-0.44), suggesting that increased solicitation effort is reflected in reduced bodyweight.
evaluation: The statistical analysis (C54-C56) provides strong evidence for the cost of solicitation, supported by Figure 6. The correlation is highly significant and consistent across time points. This finding provides a mechanistic explanation for the negative correlation between maternal provisioning and offspring solicitation (C53), though the causal interpretation requires caution as correlation does not prove causation.

result: Each BXD line is characterized by a unique combination of maternal provisioning and offspring solicitation behaviors, with levels of these traits being specific to particular genotypes. The cross-fostering design controlling for genetic variation in either mothers or offspring enabled demonstration of genotype-specific behavioral strategies.
evaluation: This conclusion (C52, C65) is supported by the overall experimental results showing genetic mapping of both maternal and offspring behaviors. However, C52 is explicitly labeled as speculative by the authors ('One scenario to explain...might be'), so while the data support genotype-specific behaviors (C65), the specific mechanism proposed (C52) remains hypothetical.

result: The authors acknowledge that postnatal cross-fostering controls for postnatal but not prenatal maternal effects, which can only be addressed by embryo transfer (impractical for genetics experiments). Prenatal maternal effects may strengthen or weaken the observed effects of offspring genotype on maternal phenotype and may contribute to phenotypic correlations between biological parents and offspring.
evaluation: This is an appropriate and important limitation acknowledged by the authors (C60-C64). The citation to Cowley et al. (1989) supports the methodological point (C60-C61). The speculation about potential confounding effects (C62-C64) is reasonable and appropriately cautious. This limitation does not invalidate the findings but indicates that the observed indirect genetic effects may include both genetic and prenatal environmental components.

result: The study addresses a gap in understanding parent-offspring conflict theory. While theory predicts that parent-offspring conflict leads to evolution of traits in offspring that influence parental behavior and vice versa, and genetic variation for such traits is assumed to exist, specific genetic variants mediating these indirect effects had not been previously identified.
evaluation: The theoretical background (C1-C6) is well-supported by appropriate citations to foundational work (Trivers 1974, Godfray 1995, Kölliker et al. 2015, Kilner and Hinde 2012, Wolf and Brodie III 1998). The identification of the knowledge gap (C7) appropriately motivates the study and is addressed by the experimental findings.

result: Prior empirical studies of parent-offspring coadaptation have found both positive correlations (in Parus major and Nicrophorus vespilloides) and negative correlations (in Sehirus cinctus) between offspring solicitation and parental provisioning traits, with coadaptation models making specific predictions about these correlations.
evaluation: The review of prior work (C44-C46) is appropriately cited and provides context for interpreting the negative correlation found in this study. The citations to multiple empirical studies (Kölliker et al. 2000, Lock et al. 2004, Agrawal et al. 2001) and theoretical work support the claim that both positive and negative correlations have been observed.
